prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The

outputs.L2:
A processor-based system creates a publicly accessible ring protected through fully homomorphic encryption. The processor first constructs a ring presentation \(G\), given by

\[
G=\langle x,y \mid x^{2}=0,\; y^{2}=0,\; xy+(p+1)yx=1\rangle,
\]

where \(x\) and \(y\) are generators and \(p\) is a first private prime.

The processor also forms an alternative presentation \(H\) of the same ring:

\[
H=\langle x,y,t \mid x^{2}=0,\; y^{2}=0,\; t=m_{1}yx,\; xy+m_{2}yx+t=1\rangle.
\]

Here, \(t\) is an additional generator, \(m_{1}\) and \(m_{2}\) are positive integers satisfying

\[
p+1=m_{1}+m_{2},
\]

and the presentations \(G\) and \(H\) are isomorphic.

The system then derives a fully homomorphically encrypted public ring \(\widehat{H}\), defined by

\[
\widehat{H}
=
\left\langle
x,y,t
\;\middle|\;
N\cdot 1=1,\;
x^{2}=1,\;
y^{2}=0,\;
xyx=x,\;
yxy=y,\;
tx=0,\;
yt=0,\;
t^{2}=t+\frac{m_{2}^{2}-m_{2}}{m_{1}}\,tyx
\right\rangle,
\]

where \(N=pq\) and \(q\) is a second private prime. The encrypted ring \(\widehat{H}\) is made publicly available. A corresponding procedure for carrying out these operations is disclosed as well.
outputs.L3:
A processor-based system first generates an initial ring presentation \(G\) from the generators \(x\) and \(y\), using a privately held prime number \(p\). The system then generates a second ring presentation \(H\) by introducing an additional generator \(t\) and selecting positive integers \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) such that

\[
p+1=m_1+m_2.
\]

The defining relations of \(H\) are chosen so that \(H\) is isomorphic to \(G\). Thus, although the two presentations use different generators and relations, they represent rings having the same algebraic structure.

The system next selects a second private prime \(q\) and computes the composite modulus

\[
N=pq.
\]

Using this modulus and the specified algebraic relations, the system constructs a fully homomorphically encrypted public ring, denoted by \(\hat{H}\). This encrypted ring permits supported ring operations to be carried out on encrypted elements while preserving the corresponding algebraic behavior of the underlying ring.

Finally, \(\hat{H}\) is published or otherwise made available for public use, while the primes \(p\) and \(q\) remain private. A corresponding method for producing the public encrypted ring—including the generation of \(G\) and \(H\), the selection of \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), and the construction of \(\hat{H}\) modulo \(N\)—is also disclosed.
outputs.L4:
The processor begins by selecting a private prime \(p\) and two integers \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) such that  
\[
p+1=m_1+m_2.
\]
Using these private values together with a prescribed collection of generators and relations, it constructs two presentations of a ring. Although the presentations may use different generators or encode the relations in different forms, they define isomorphic rings. An explicit or efficiently computable isomorphism between them ensures that elements and operations can be translated consistently from one presentation to the other.

The processor then chooses a second private prime \(q\) and forms the composite modulus  
\[
N=pq.
\]
Information derived from the two private presentations is transferred into a public ring defined relative to \(N\). The public description permits users to represent ring elements and carry out the supported addition and multiplication operations without revealing the factorization of \(N\), the prime \(p\), the auxiliary prime \(q\), or the private decomposition \(p+1=m_1+m_2\).

The public ring is released in encrypted form under a fully homomorphic encryption mechanism. Consequently, authorized computations can be evaluated directly on encrypted representations of its elements and structure. The resulting ciphertexts decrypt to the same values that would have been obtained by performing the corresponding ring operations on the underlying plaintext data. Thus, the construction provides a publicly usable computational interface while keeping the prime parameters and private presentations hidden.

The intended security rests on the secrecy of \(p\) and \(q\), the difficulty of recovering them from \(N\), and the security assumptions of the fully homomorphic encryption scheme. In practice, the construction must also specify the exact generators, relations, isomorphisms, encoding procedures, key-generation algorithm, and noise-management mechanism before its correctness and security can be formally established.
outputs.L5:
**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the most frequently used words in the English language. Known as the definite article, it identifies a specific person, place, object, or idea. For example, “a book” can refer to any book, while “the book” points to one particular book understood by both the speaker and the listener.

Although it consists of only three letters, “the” brings clarity and precision to communication. It helps distinguish what is known from what is general and connects sentences to their context. This small word demonstrates how even the simplest elements of language can carry great importance.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent abstract for a system and method that produces a publicly available, fully homomorphically encrypted ring using two isomorphic ring presentations and private primes p and q.
counterfactuals.output: A computer-implemented system and method provide a publicly accessible encrypted ring supporting homomorphic evaluation. A key-generation process selects private primes \(p\) and \(q\), forms a composite modulus derived therefrom, and constructs first and second ring presentations that are isomorphic while differing in their public representations. A secret key includes \(p\), \(q\), and information defining or efficiently recovering an isomorphism between the ring presentations. Public parameters expose the second ring presentation, an encoding procedure, and operations for addition and multiplication of encoded elements without revealing corresponding plaintext elements or the private primes. A plaintext element represented in the first ring presentation is mapped to an encrypted representative in the second ring presentation. Repeated public addition and multiplication of encrypted representatives produce a representative that, upon application of a private inverse mapping or decryption procedure, corresponds to the same ring expression evaluated on the plaintext elements. Optional rerandomization, validity testing, and noise-management procedures preserve representation security and support arbitrary-depth homomorphic computation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the disclosed cryptographic invention involving the ring presentations G and H, the relation p+1=m1+m2, and the public encrypted ring Ĥ where N=pq.
counterfactuals.output:
The invention describes a public-key cryptosystem built by hiding the structure of one finitely presented ring inside another.

- Two related ring presentations, \(G\) and \(H\), are constructed using secret parameters, including integers \(m_1,m_2\) chosen so that
  \[
  p+1=m_1+m_2.
  \]
- A second secret prime \(q\) is selected and the composite modulus
  \[
  N=pq
  \]
  is formed.
- The presentation of \(H\) is then transformed or “encrypted” to produce a public ring \(\widehat H\) over the composite modulus. Its generators and relations conceal the recognizable structure of \(H\) and its correspondence with \(G\).
- Public users perform encryption using computations in \(\widehat H\). The key owner, knowing \(p,q\), the parameters \(m_1,m_2\), and the hidden transformations between the presentations, can reduce or decompose the computation—typically using the two prime components of \(N\)—and recover the encoded message.
- Security is intended to come from the difficulty of reconstructing the hidden ring presentation or correspondence without the trapdoor, together with the difficulty of factoring \(N\).

Thus, \(\widehat H\) functions as an obfuscated public algebraic object, while the factorization of \(N\) and the structural relationship among \(G\), \(H\), \(m_1\), and \(m_2\) form the private decryption trapdoor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Convert these mathematical claims into a formal invention abstract: G=⟨x,y | x²=0, y²=0, xy+(p+1)yx=1⟩; H=⟨x,y,t | x²=0, y²=0, t=m1yx, xy+m2yx+t=1⟩; p+1=m1+m2; and N=pq.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

Disclosed is a computer-implemented method for constructing an algebraic representation associated with an integer \(N\). The method receives integers \(p\) and \(q\) satisfying \(N=pq\), selects parameters \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) satisfying \(p+1=m_1+m_2\), and defines generators \(x\) and \(y\) subject to the relations \(x^2=0\), \(y^2=0\), and \(xy+(p+1)yx=1\), thereby forming an algebraic structure \(G\). An extended algebraic structure \(H\) is formed by introducing a generator \(t\) subject to \(t=m_1yx\) and \(xy+m_2yx+t=1\), while retaining the nilpotency relations \(x^2=0\) and \(y^2=0\). Substitution of \(t=m_1yx\) and \(p+1=m_1+m_2\) establishes equivalence between the defining mixed-generator relations of \(G\) and \(H\). The construction provides a parameterized representation in which the coefficient \(p+1\) is decomposed into independently specified components \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), enabling symbolic manipulation, verification, and computational analysis of algebraic relations associated with the factorization \(N=pq\).
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a cryptographic system for public-ring fully homomorphic encryption in the style of a U.S. patent abstract, specifying the processor, private primes, generators, isomorphic ring presentations, public ring relations, and corresponding method.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract—** A computer-implemented public-ring fully homomorphic encryption system includes at least one processor and memory storing instructions that cause the processor to generate a plurality of private primes \(p_1,\ldots,p_t\), select respective generators \(g_i\) of designated cyclic subgroups over \(\mathbb F_{p_i}\), and construct a private ring presentation  
\[
R_{\mathrm{priv}}=\prod_{i=1}^{t}\mathbb F_{p_i}[X]/(f_i(X)),
\]
where each \(f_i\) is selected using the corresponding generator \(g_i\). The processor further generates a public ring presentation  
\[
R_{\mathrm{pub}}=\mathbb Z[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]/I_{\mathrm{pub}},
\]
together with a secret isomorphism, or efficiently invertible family of component isomorphisms, between a bounded-noise subset of \(R_{\mathrm{pub}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{priv}}\). The ideal \(I_{\mathrm{pub}}\) is published as public ring relations comprising randomized polynomial relations that preserve addition and multiplication while concealing the private primes, generators, factors, and change-of-presentation maps. A public key identifies \(R_{\mathrm{pub}}\), the public relations, encoding parameters, and evaluation or refresh data; a secret key includes the private primes and information sufficient to recover the private presentation and inverse isomorphism. Encryption maps a plaintext into redundant private-ring components, adds bounded error, and transports the resulting encoding into the public presentation. Homomorphic addition and multiplication are performed by reducing public-ring expressions modulo \(I_{\mathrm{pub}}\). A refresh operation homomorphically evaluates a decryption-and-reencoding circuit, optionally using key-switching and modulus-management data, thereby permitting evaluation of circuits of unbounded depth. Decryption applies the secret inverse presentation, reduces the recovered components with respect to the private primes and generators, and reconstructs the plaintext. Corresponding methods and non-transitory computer-readable media for key generation, encryption, public-ring evaluation, refreshing, and decryption are also disclosed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
